The first was for a presentation on the affordability of the solutions put forward by the project team. The UDERMS team highlighted that more than 70 percent of housing units are designated affordable, with facilities modeling 30–50 percent energy savings compared to prevailing construction practices. The project demonstrated that centralized systems, right-sized DER deployments, and smart energy management can lower capital and operating expenses while providing consumer choice at reduced cost. This was delivered in April 2025. The second was a Data Brief, requested to show how the project team was progressing in M&V plan completion. The UDERMS team reported on the collection of data from over 1,300 DER devices and over 700 AMI meters across Salt Lake City, Logan, and Ogden, with semi-automated ETL processes built around a schema and a relational database architecture that directly links data types to required LBNL metrics. Data snapshots were provided for PV, BESS, EVSE, and energy efficiency calculations. This was delivered in May 2025. 6.1.8 Task 8.0: Evaluate Grid Services for DERs The goal of this task was to evaluate techniques for enabling grid services for multiple time scales spanning peak load management, ancillary services, and frequency response. The techniques include network-flow, time- extended resource allocation schemes that consider the real-time load requirements and generation capabilities of the individual DERs, and localized, market-based auction schemes to adjust load scheduling of rapid flexible DERs to meet the current energy generation. These solutions were evaluated at the USU microgrid testing facility and iterated using hardware-in-the-loop for improvements in performance and robustness prior to production level deployment in PacifiCorp’s EMS in BP3. The specific supporting subtasks include: - Subtask 8.1.0: Evaluate DER control strategy, architecture, and communications - Subtask 8.2.0: Implement HIL models of distribution grid and DER - Subtask 8.3.0: Iterate control algorithms There were several actions taken to evaluate and iterate the grid services including (1) development of control parameters; (2) automation definition; (3) telecommunication and integration requirements; (4) development and testing in the test environment of the EMS with the OSI Monarch and Integra DERMS solution; and (5) DER definition and configuration requirements within the software. 16 6.1.8.1 Subtask 8.1.0: Evaluate DER control strategy, architecture, and communications 6.1.8.1.1 Overview of Control Strategy, Architecture and Communications Executing the defined UDERMS grid services across diverse devices at each project site required careful planning and documentation of the control strategy, architecture, and communications. The network architecture diagram below shows how a shed signal, originating from the DERMS server that is housed in the sandbox environment at PacifiCorp (PAC)’s Rocky Mountain Power (RMP) location, arrives at each controlled device type at each site. Figure 1: Network Architecture Diagram 17 OpenADR was leveraged as the main integration protocol before translating to device-specific protocols downstream. There was also a second control signal originating from the “Grid Side” that steams from the production DERMS platform using a DNP3 signal to control the Sonnen battery energy storage systems (BESS).
